checks.source_claim: Accepted author manuscript PDF 11 (manuscript 10), equation (2.6) and footnote 7, under the nonnegative even L1 assumptions on PDF 4-5; downstream (2.7)-(2.8) on PDF 12.
checks.independent_reasoning: Take n=1, f0(y)=exp(-|y|)/2, a=exp(t), sigma^2=1-exp(-2t). The OU formula gives ft(z)=a E exp(-a|z-sigma Z|)/2. Then exp(az)ft(z)<=C=(a/2)exp(a^2 sigma^2/2), and dominated convergence as z tends to +infinity gives limit C. Thus the supremum is C, ft-polar(a)=1/C>0, but F_t^(p)(a)=integral (exp(az)ft(z))^(1/p) dz is infinite for every p in (0,1), so its qth power is zero. At t=log 2 the mismatch is zero versus exp(-3/2). This is an admissible even integrable input and disproves both the all-x limit and claimed automatic Gaussian upper tail.
checks.counterevidence_and_impact: For D={x:sup_z exp(<x,z>)ft(z)<infinity}, convexity follows from the geometric mean inequality. Interior points have an integrable exponential envelope using x +/- delta e_i; the L^r to L-infinity limit holds there. Outside D, continuity and unbounded supremum give the zero polar limit. The convex boundary is null if D has full dimension, while D itself is null otherwise. Hence an almost-everywhere formulation suffices. The positive lower bound for ft on a cube supplies the integrable majorant used in (2.8); no Gaussian upper tail is needed for that step. The local claim is false, but the stated repair preserves the integral passage and does not refute the main monotonicity theorem.

checks.source_claim: Accepted author manuscript PDF 13 (manuscript 12), the lower inequalities in (2.11), after reduction to bounded compactly supported even initial data.
checks.independent_reasoning: The admissible even density f0=1[-1,1]/2 becomes smooth and even under positive-time OU evolution, so ft'(0)=0. A positive c1 times the Gaussian factor in the displayed lower bound is strictly positive at zero. Therefore the asserted lower bound for |gradient ft| cannot hold. The counterexample lies within the additional compact-support reduction, not merely the broader theorem assumptions.
checks.counterevidence_and_impact: Only a positive Gaussian lower bound for ft itself is required. For t in a compact positive-time interval, bounded initial support and the OU kernel give Gaussian upper bounds with polynomial factors for ft, gradient ft and Laplacian ft, while a positive-mass bounded subset gives a lower Gaussian bound for ft. The impossible derivative lower bounds are not used in the subsequent integrations. Retain a local Minor, not a failure of the main theorem.

checks.source_claim: Accepted author manuscript PDF 13, the expansion of L_z[exp(<x,z>/p)ft^(1/p-1)] following (2.11); continuation and (2.12) on PDF 14.
checks.independent_reasoning: Write alpha=1/p-1 and ell=log ft. Direct differentiation for L=Delta-z dot gradient gives Lw=w[|x|^2/p^2+(2alpha/p)x dot gradient ell+alpha^2|gradient ell|^2+alpha Delta ell-x dot z/p-alpha z dot gradient ell], with w=exp(<x,z>/p)ft^alpha. Thus the Delta log ft term must have the same ft^alpha prefactor; the printed ft^(1/p-2) is wrong. This is not rendered vacuous by the input assumptions: for f0=1[-1,1]/2, t=log 2 and p=1/2 at x=z=0, each OU kernel center lies in [-1/2,1/2] with variance 3/4, so ft''(0)<0 and ft(0)<1. The printed and correct terms differ.
checks.counterevidence_and_impact: The immediately following integrated display already uses the correct ft^(1/p) Delta log ft factor, and (2.12) has the corresponding correct identity. The retained independent symbolic result is reused with its original execution attribution; the differentiation above is the present executor's independent check. No downstream failure is established, so Minor is appropriate.
